figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Samples generated by CogVideo. The actual text inputs are in Chinese. Each sample is a 4-second clip of 32 frames, and here we sample 9 frames uniformly for display purposes. More samples, models and codes will be available at https://github.com/THUDM/CogVideo.
figures.headline: Nine sampled frames from each 4-second, 32-frame CogVideo clip, generated from Chinese text prompts, show high-resolution output.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 1, CogVideo can generate high-resolution (480$\times$480) videos.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Multi-frame-rate hierarchical generation framework in CogVideo. Input sequence includes frame rate, text, frame tokens. [B] (Begin-of-image) is a separator token, inherited from CogView2. In stage 1, $T_{s}$ frames are generated sequentially on condition of frame rate and text. Then in stage 2, generated frames are re-input as bidirectional attention regions to recursively interpolate frames. Frame rate can be adjusted during both stages. Bidirectional attention regions are highlighted in blue, and unidirectional regions are highlighted in green.
figures.headline: Stage 1 generates 5 key frames from frame rate and text, and Stage 2 recursively interpolates the frames between them.
citing_sentences: The multi-frame-rate hierarchical generation is a recursive process, illustrated in Figure 2.
As shown in 2, (1) all frames in stage 1 and the 2nd, 4th frames in stage 2 are in the unidirectional region; (2) {Frame Rate}, {Text} and all other frames belong to the bidirectional region.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The dual-channel attention block. We initialize the Attention-plus the same as Attention-base so that the model behaves exactly the same as CogView2 when it is initialized.
figures.headline: The dual-channel attention block adds an attention-plus channel initialized to match attention-base, so the model starts identical to CogView2.
citing_sentences: All the parameters in the CogView2 are frozen in the training, and only the parameters in the newly added attention layer (See the attention-plus in Figure 3) are trainable.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: In 3D autoregressive swin attention (window size $2\times 2$ as an example), the token in the red box can only attend to (either directly or indirectly) the yellow or green tokens. The gray tokens in the $i$-th frame and the token in the red box can be generated in parallel.
figures.headline: Shifted window autoregressive attention lets some tokens in later frames be generated in parallel with earlier frames before those frames finish.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 4, we can start generating parts of the tokens in the following frames before finishing the generation of all the previous frames — they can work in parallel.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Human evaluation results. “CogVideo 1Stage” refers to the method in ablation study, which only generates videos sequentially with the CogVideo’s Stage 1 to the desired number of frames.
figures.headline: CogVideo scores higher than VideoGPT, TGANv2, and the one-stage variant on frame texture, motion realism, and semantic relevance.
citing_sentences: Results in Figure 5 show that CogVideo significantly outperforms baselines on multiple important aspects including frame texture, motion realism and semantic relevance, and achieves the top score by the overall quality.
As shown in Figure 5, the hierarchical model, i.e. CogVideo, outperforms the 1-stage model on semantic relevance, motion realism as well as texture quality.
Results of the human evaluation, including the average score and standard deviation for each group, have already been introduced in Figure 5 in the main body.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Training loss in ablation study.
figures.headline: Training loss falls faster when CogVideo starts from CogView2 weights than when it starts from random initialization.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 plots the training loss curve of (1) finetuning CogVideo; (2) training model from random initialization; (3) training model initialized with CogView2 and partially fixed.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Video samples in ablation study, which are generated priming on the class label and first 5 frames in Kinetics-600. All samples are downsampled by extracting one in every three frames for display purposes. (a) Use finetuned CogVideo to hierarchically generate samples. (b) Train a model on Kinetics-600 which is initialized as and partially fixed to CogView2, and hierarchically generate samples. (c) Train a model on Kinetics-600 which is randomly initialized, and hierarchically generate samples. (d)(e) Use finetuned CogVideo to generate frames in 1 stage with different $N_{overlap}$.
figures.headline: Randomly initialized samples show irrational deformation, while CogView2-initialized and hierarchical CogVideo samples look more realistic.
citing_sentences: Qualitative comparison is shown in Figure 7.
This is probably because the 1-stage model cannot estimate a proper intensity of change from the previous frames in the window, as shown in Figure 7(d)(e).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: The attention distribution among frames and texts in sequential generation (Stage 1). Only 24 of 48 attention heads in 6 layers are selected for display purposes. Each attention head is visualized with a heat map of size 5$\times$6, where lighter color represents larger value. The 5$\times$5 block on the left indicates the sum of attention scores (after softmax) between each pair of frames, and the rightmost column indicates the sum of the attention score of each frame to text. That is to say, the grid in row i column j ($j\leq 5$) represents $\sum_{x\in F_{i},y\in F_{j}}\text{attn}_{x,y}$, and the grid in row i column 6 represents $\sum_{x\in F_{i},y\in T}\text{attn}_{x,y}$, where $F_{i}$, $T$ denotes the set of tokens in the i-th frame and text respectively, and $\text{attn}_{x,y}$ denotes the attention score of token x to y.
figures.headline: Stage 1 attention heads focus on text, on one frame, or across several frames, with higher layers attending more to text.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 visualizes the distribution among frames and texts in sequential generation (Stage 1) with heat maps, where only 24 of 48 attention heads in 6 layers are shown for display purposes.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: The scale factor $\alpha$ controlling the ratio between the spatial and temporal channel in equation 1 in dual-channel attention. Only $\alpha$ in half of the layers are shown for display reasons. As $\alpha$ is a vector of dimension 3072, we show the mean and variance among all of its dimensions in this figure.
figures.headline: Scale factor alpha, shown as mean and variance over dimensions, indicates heavy reliance on CogView2's spatial channel features.
citing_sentences: We further illustrate this perspective with Figure 9, which shows that features calculated by CogView2 in the spatial channel are heavily relied on.

abstract: Large-scale pretrained transformers have created milestones in text (GPT-3) and text-to-image (DALL-E and CogView) generation. Its application to video generation is still facing many challenges: The potential huge computation cost makes the training from scratch unaffordable; The scarcity and weak relevance of text-video datasets hinder the model understanding complex movement semantics. In this work, we present 9B-parameter transformer CogVideo, trained by inheriting a pretrained text-to-image model, CogView2. We also propose multi-frame-rate hierarchical training strategy to better align text and video clips. As (probably) the first open-source large-scale pretrained text-to-video model, CogVideo outperforms all publicly available models at a large margin in machine and human evaluations.

sections.body: The introduction argues that autoregressive transformers that work for text-to-image generation struggle with text-video generation. It names two causes: the largest annotated text-video dataset, VATEX, has only 41,250 videos, and fixed-length clipping breaks the link between a text prompt and its matching motion. CogVideo has 9.4 billion parameters, is trained on 5.4 million text-video pairs, and is built on the pretrained text-to-image model CogView2. It uses multi-frame-rate hierarchical training, which picks the lowest frame rate at which the clip still holds the complete action, and it generates 480×480 videos. The authors claim it is the first open-source pretrained transformer of this kind in the general domain.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Scarce text-video data and fixed-length clipping weaken text-action alignment, so the paper proposes CogVideo.

sections.body: The section reviews video generation, from deterministic next-frame predictors such as CDNA and PredRNN to GAN-based methods such as VGAN, TGAN and MoCoGAN, and then to text-to-video models. It states that earlier methods were trained on specific datasets such as UCF-101 and that most of these models are not publicly available. For autoregressive transformers, it notes that GODIVA and NÜWA generate frames one by one in chronological order, which the authors say may cause poor text-video alignment. The section reports no experiments of its own; its alignment claims refer back to the introduction.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier video generators used narrow datasets and were mostly not public; recent autoregressive ones may misalign text and frames.

sections.body: The method has three parts. Multi-frame-rate hierarchical training adds a frame-rate token to the text, samples each video at the lowest frame rate that yields at least 5 frames, and generates 5 key frames sequentially before recursively interpolating the middle frames. Dual-channel attention adds a trainable spatial-temporal attention channel to each CogView2 transformer layer, while all CogView2 parameters stay frozen. The section also extends Swin attention to autoregressive video generation, which lets tokens in different frames be generated in parallel. The section reports no experimental numbers for these choices.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Multi-frame-rate training, dual-channel attention on frozen CogView2 weights, and shifted window attention together form the CogVideo method.

sections.body: The backbone has 48 layers, a hidden size of 3,072 in each attention channel, 48 attention heads, and 9.4 billion parameters, of which 6 billion are fixed to CogView2's parameters. The fixed parameters cover the feed-forward networks, the spatial attention channel, the first frame's positional embeddings, and all image and text vocabulary embeddings. Both stages use sequences of 2,065 tokens: 64 text tokens, 5 frames of 400 image tokens each, and one separator token. Videos are at 160×160 and are upsampled to 480×480 by CogView2. Parameters are updated by Adam with beta1 0.9 and beta2 0.95.
sections.heading: Training
sections.headline: Training uses a 48-layer, 9.4 billion parameter transformer on 5.4 million captioned videos with Adam optimization.

sections.body: Machine evaluation uses UCF101 and Kinetics-600 with Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) and Inception score (IS). On UCF101, CogVideo has IS 50.46 and FVD 626, against DIGAN's FVD of 577 and TATS-base's IS of 79.28. On Kinetics-600, CogVideo has FVD 109.23 (59.55 when the ground truth is the tokenizer reconstruction), which is better than Latent Video Transformer's 224.73 and Video Transformer's 170, but worse than DVD-GAN-FP's 69.15 and TriVD-GAN-FP's 25.74. In human evaluation with 90 completed evaluators, CogVideo was chosen as best in 49.53% of cases, against 15.42% for VideoGPT and 5.6% for TGANv2. Kinetics frames are center-cropped and downsampled to 64×64 for FVD.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: CogVideo beats two baselines on Fréchet distance on Kinetics-600 but trails other baselines on several measures.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that CogVideo reuses a pretrained text-to-image model, avoids training from scratch, and uses multi-frame-rate hierarchical training to improve text-video understanding and control the intensity of change. It says that extending Swin attention to CogLM speeds up both training and inference. It names a limitation: input sequence length is restricted by model size and GPU memory, which is left for future work. The Broader Impact paragraph says the work could ease short-video and digital art creation and could reduce energy consumption and carbon emission by avoiding training from scratch. It names misinformation as a negative impact and proposes an additional classifier to detect fakes.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors call CogVideo the first open-source pretrained text-to-video transformer and note that input length remains limited.

sections.body: This acknowledgments section thanks named colleagues for help with data collection, for useful discussions, and for maintaining the machines. It also credits the computational resources supported by BAAI. It contains no methods, results, or limitations, so no claims from the paper are made here.
sections.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
sections.headline: The section acknowledges collaborators for data collection, discussion, machine maintenance, and computing resources.

sections.body: Appendix A visualizes Stage 1 attention for 24 of 48 heads in 6 layers and finds that many temporal-channel heads give little attention to the frame itself, which the authors read as partial decoupling of temporal and spatial analysis. Appendix B gives training details: each stage has 7.7 billion parameters, with 6 billion of them fixed to CogView2, for 9.4 billion in total. Stage 1 is pretrained for 76,000 iterations at 0.25 fps and then 15,000 iterations at 1 fps, while Stage 2 runs 78,500 iterations at 2, 4, and 8 fps, with batch size 416. Appendix C describes human evaluation: 30 UCF-101 classes, 90 evaluators who completed the task, scores from 1 to 5 on three aspects, and a 1 to 10 overall quality score.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix analyzes attention heads and the scale factor, and lists stage training details and the human evaluation protocol.
